lines.text: Automation and advanced manufacturing use computers, robots, and 3D printers to build accurate parts.
In conventional turning and drilling, a worker turns handwheels, measures by hand, and relies on skill.
A CNC machine uses a computer controller to guide tools automatically from a stored program.
Compared to manual machines, CNC costs more upfront, yet delivers high repeatability and complex shapes.
CNC serves auto, aerospace, and medical parts using turning centres for round shafts and machining centres for flat or 3D cuts.
Inside, a controller drives axis motors, checks feedback sensors, and tracks X, Y, and Z coordinates.
Part programs combine G-codes like G01 for straight cuts with M-codes like M03 to spin the spindle.
CNC reduces idle time, simplifies fixtures, and adapts fast, though maintenance and skilled coders cost more.
Industrial robots are programmable arms that repeat exact motion patterns until reprogrammed for a new job.
They handle materials, load machines, weld, spray paint, carve, assemble, and inspect parts nonstop.
Additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, builds parts layer by layer directly from a 3D CAD model.
Material extrusion melts plastic through a hot nozzle, while vat photopolymerization cures liquid resin with UV light.
Every 3D print follows four steps: create the CAD file, slice into layers, print, and post-process.
Slicer layer height trades detail for speed: thin layers look smoother, while thick layers finish faster.
Infill controls internal strength using Grid, Triangles, Gyroid, or Honeycomb patterns at ten to forty percent.
Balanced print speed prevents vibration, nozzle heat melts filament cleanly, and a warm bed prevents warping.
Overhangs past forty five degrees need supports, though smart part orientation reduces waste and cleanup.
Together, CNC, robotics, and 3D printing turn digital ideas into reliable physical products.
